parent_reference.heading: 2. Definition
parent_reference.content:
A chess board is a square board divided into 64 smaller squares arranged in an 8×8 grid. The squares alternate between two colors — one light, one dark. Each player sits on opposite sides of the board. The board is the playing field for every game of chess.

---

parent_reference.heading: 3. Why It Matters
parent_reference.content:
Every chess concept your child will ever learn happens on this board. If they cannot orient the board correctly or find specific squares, every future lesson becomes harder. Think of it this way: you would not teach someone to read without first showing them the alphabet. The chess board is the alphabet of chess. Children who are comfortable with the board learn piece movement, tactics, and strategy much faster because they are not struggling with the basics underneath.

parent_reference.heading: 5. Parent Understands
parent_reference.content:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it. You need to know this before you can teach it.*

**The 64 Squares**
The board has exactly 64 squares: 32 light and 32 dark, arranged in an alternating checkerboard pattern. No two squares of the same color are ever next to each other (horizontally or vertically).

**Board Orientation**
This is the single most common setup mistake. The board must be placed so that **the bottom-right corner square (closest to each player's right hand) is a light-colored square**. An easy way to remember: **"Light on Right."** If the corner square on your right is dark, the board is turned the wrong way.

**Files, Ranks, and Coordinates**
- **Files** are the vertical columns running up and down the board. They are labeled **a** through **h** from left to right (from White's perspective).
- **Ranks** are the horizontal rows running side to side. They are numbered **1** through **8** from bottom to top (from White's perspective).
- Every square has a unique name made from its file letter and rank number. For example, the bottom-left corner is **a1** and the top-right corner is **h8**.

**Piece Placement**
Each side starts with 16 pieces arranged on the two ranks closest to them:
- **Rank 1 (White) / Rank 8 (Black)**: Rook, Knight, Bishop, Queen, King, Bishop, Knight, Rook.
- **Rank 2 (White) / Rank 7 (Black)**: All eight pawns.

The critical rule: **"Queen on her own color."** The White Queen goes on the light square (d1). The Black Queen goes on the dark square (d8).

---

parent_reference.heading: 6. How to Teach It
parent_reference.content:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — Start with the empty board (2 minutes)
Place the empty board between you and your child. Say:

> *"This is a chess board. It has 64 squares — can you see how the colors take turns? Light, dark, light, dark. Let's count one row together."*

Let them count one row (they should get 8).

### Step 2 — Teach "Light on Right" (1 minute)
Point to the bottom-right corner. Ask:

> *"What color is this corner? It should always be light. Remember: Light on Right."*

Turn the board wrong, then ask them to fix it. Repeat until they do it automatically.

### Step 3 — Introduce the corners (2 minutes)
Place one piece in each corner. Say:

> *"The Rooks — the castle towers — always go in the corners. Can you put one in each corner?"*

### Step 4 — Build from the outside in (3 minutes)
Work from corners toward center:

> *"Next to each Rook, place a Knight — the horse. Then next to each Knight, place a Bishop. Now we just have two squares left in the middle. That's where the Queen and King go."*

### Step 5 — Teach "Queen on her color" (2 minutes)
Hold up the White Queen. Point to d1:

> *"The Queen always goes on her own color. White Queen on the white square. Can you show me?"*

Do the same for the Black Queen on d8.

### Step 6 — Place the pawns (1 minute)
> *"Now fill the whole second row with pawns — the little soldiers who protect everyone."*

### Step 7 — Celebrate
> *"You just set up a chess board! Every grandmaster in the world starts their game exactly like this."*

parent_reference.heading: 7. Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
parent_reference.content:
> **🏰 The Castle Analogy**
>
> Imagine the chess board is a castle's courtyard — a big square field made of tiles. The tiles alternate between white marble and dark stone, like a grand checkerboard floor. Two armies face each other from opposite ends of the courtyard. The generals (Kings) stand in the center with their advisors (Queens), protected by towers (Rooks) in the corners, horsemen (Knights) next to the towers, and the royal guards (Bishops) beside them. In front of the whole army stands a row of brave soldiers (Pawns), ready to march forward.
>
> **Memory tricks your child will love:**
> - **"Light on Right"** — Say it every time you set up the board together.
> - **"Queen on her color"** — The White Queen likes the white tile. The Black Queen likes the dark tile.
> - **"Rooks in the corners, like castle towers"** — Rooks look like towers and they go in the corners, just like real towers on a castle wall.

parent_reference.heading: 8. Did You Know? 🎓
parent_reference.content:
The chess board we use today has been virtually unchanged for over **500 years**. The 8×8 grid was standardized in Europe during the 15th century, though chess itself is over 1,400 years old. Some early versions of the game were played on 10×10 boards! When your child sets up their board, they are continuing a tradition that stretches back centuries — longer than most countries have existed.

*Share this with your child: "Did you know this board design is over 500 years old? Even kings and queens in castles played on a board just like this one!"*

parent_reference.heading: 10. How It Works
parent_reference.content:
### Setting Up the Board — Step by Step

1. **Place the board** so that a **light square** is in the bottom-right corner ("Light on Right").
2. **Place the Rooks** in all four corners: a1, h1 (White), a8, h8 (Black).
3. **Place the Knights** next to each Rook: b1, g1 (White), b8, g8 (Black).
4. **Place the Bishops** next to each Knight: c1, f1 (White), c8, f8 (Black).
5. **Place the Queens** — "Queen on her own color": d1 (White Queen on the light square), d8 (Black Queen on the dark square).
6. **Place the Kings** on the remaining center square: e1 (White), e8 (Black).
7. **Place all Pawns** on the second rank: a2 through h2 (White), a7 through h7 (Black).

![DGM-004 Back Rank Guide](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-001/DGM-004_Back_Rank_Guide.svg)

*Tip: Teach your child the order from the outside in — Rooks first (corners), then Knights, then Bishops, then Queen and King in the center.*

### Key Rules
- The board has **8 files** (columns, labeled a–h) and **8 ranks** (rows, numbered 1–8).
- **Light on Right**: The bottom-right corner must always be a light square.
- **Queen on her own color**: White Queen on a light square (d1), Black Queen on a dark square (d8).
- Both armies **mirror each other** across the board.

parent_reference.heading: 12. Real Game Example
parent_reference.content:
**Every chess game ever played in history started from this exact position.**

In the 2013 World Chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Viswanathan Anand, the board was set up exactly as shown in Diagram 1 — with "Light on Right" and "Queen on her own color." Whether it is a game between two world champions or your child's first game at the kitchen table, the starting position is always the same.

This is one of the beautiful things about chess: the rules have been the same for hundreds of years. When your child sets up the board correctly, they are doing the exact same thing that every grandmaster has done.

*Tell your child: "You just set up the board the same way Magnus Carlsen does. That's pretty cool."*

parent_reference.heading: 13. Common Mistakes
parent_reference.content:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Board rotated 90°** — A dark square ends up in the bottom-right corner. Fix: "Light on Right."
- ❌ **King and Queen swapped** — The most frequent error. Fix: "Queen on her own color."
- ❌ **Knights and Bishops swapped** — Knights go next to the Rooks (on b and g files), Bishops go next to the Queen and King (on c and f files).
- ❌ **Rooks not in the corners** — Rooks are always on the a-file and h-file.

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Naming all pieces at once** — This overwhelms a young child. Start with the board itself, then introduce pieces one at a time over multiple sessions if needed.
- ❌ **Correcting mistakes harshly** — Setup errors are normal. Gently guide rather than point out failures.
- ❌ **Skipping board orientation** — Many parents jump straight to pieces. Always start with "Light on Right."

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If your child keeps swapping the King and Queen, try this: let them place only the Queen first, every time, before any other piece. Once the Queen is on her color, the King automatically gets the only square left. This builds the habit faster than correcting the mistake.

parent_reference.heading: 14. Teaching Notes
parent_reference.content:
**For the parent / coach:**

- **Teach this before** introducing any piece movement. The board must feel familiar first.
- **Use a physical board first.** Screen-based boards are fine later, but the tactile experience of picking up pieces and placing them helps young children remember.
- **Let your child touch and explore.** Let them pick up pieces, feel them, and ask questions before you start the "lesson."
- **Break it into sessions if needed.** Session 1: Board orientation and squares. Session 2: Piece placement. There is no rush.

**Questions to ask your child:**
- "Which corner should be light?" (Bottom-right)
- "Where does the Queen go?" (On her own color)
- "What goes in the corners?" (The Rooks)
- "How many squares are on the board?" (64)

**Signs your child understands:**
- They orient the board correctly without help.
- They place the Queen on the right square.
- They say "Light on Right" unprompted.

**Signs they need more practice:**
- They consistently place the Queen on the wrong square.
- They rotate the board incorrectly.
- They confuse Knights and Bishops.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> The single best drill for this topic is the "blind setup" — cover the board with a cloth, ask your child to set up one side from memory, then reveal and check together. This moves knowledge from recognition to recall.

parent_reference.heading: 15. Parent FAQ
parent_reference.content:
**Q: My child keeps placing the board wrong. Should I keep correcting them?**
A: Yes, gently. Say "Let's check — Light on Right!" and let them fix it themselves. Avoid saying "That's wrong." Instead, make it a quick game: "Quick quiz — is this corner light?" Within a few sessions, they will self-correct automatically.

**Q: Do I need to teach coordinates (a1, b2, etc.) right away?**
A: Not immediately. Your child should first be comfortable with the board itself — its colors, its orientation, and where the pieces go. Coordinates are a separate topic (TOP-006) that builds on this one. Introduce them naturally over time ("Can you put the Rook on a1?") rather than as a formal lesson.

**Q: Is it okay to start with fewer pieces?**
A: Absolutely. Many coaches start by placing only pawns, or only Rooks and Kings. This reduces overwhelm and lets the child focus on fewer things at once. The full 32-piece setup is the goal, not the starting point.

parent_reference.heading: 16. Practice Together
parent_reference.content:
*These activities are designed for parent and child to do together. No scores. No pressure. Just learning.*

### 🏁 Speed Setup Race
Both parent and child each get a set of pieces. Race to set up the board correctly. The goal is not to win — it is to practice together. Cheer each other on.

### 🔍 Find the Square
Point to any square and ask your child to name it (or vice versa). Start with corners (a1, h1, a8, h8), then try center squares (d4, e5). Use the coordinates diagram below for reference.

![DGM-003 Board Coordinates](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-001/DGM-003_Board_Coordinates.svg)

### 🎨 Color Check
Remove all pieces. Point to random squares and ask: "Is this square light or dark?" Then try: "Can you find d4? What color is it?"

### 🪞 Mirror Game
Set up only White's pieces. Ask your child to "mirror" them on Black's side. This reinforces that both sides are identical reflections of each other.

### 👑 Queen Challenge
Remove just the Queens and Kings. Ask your child to place them correctly. If they say "Queen on her own color" before you do — they have mastered the most important setup rule.

---

parent_reference.heading: 17. Coach Challenge ⭐
parent_reference.content:
### 🏆 The 60-Second Setup Challenge

**Challenge your child:**

> "Can you set up the entire board correctly in under 60 seconds?"

**Rules:**
1. Start with an empty board and all 32 pieces in a pile.
2. The parent times with a phone or watch.
3. The child sets up the board.
4. When done, the parent checks: "Light on Right? Queen on her own color? Rooks in the corners?"
5. If everything is correct, record their time.

**Make it fun:**
- First attempt: just get it right, no time pressure.
- Second attempt: try to beat your first time.
- Track improvement over days — children love seeing their time drop.

*This is PCA original content. This challenge builds muscle memory for board setup while making it a game rather than a chore.*

---

parent_reference.heading: 18. Try It Yourself
parent_reference.content:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
**Look at the diagram below. Something is wrong with White's setup. Can you spot the mistake?**

![DGM-005 Puzzle](../../assets/diagrams/TOP-001/DGM-005_Puzzle_Spot_The_Mistake.svg)

*Answer: The White King and Queen are swapped. The Queen should be on d1 (light square) and the King should be on e1 (dark square). Remember: "Queen on her own color."*

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
**Without looking at any diagram, answer these three questions:**
1. What are the four corner squares of the board?
2. What color is the square h1?
3. Which piece goes on a1?

*Answers: (1) a1, h1, a8, h8. (2) Light. (3) The Rook.*

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)
**Your board has a dark square in the bottom-right corner. You have placed all 32 pieces perfectly on the board. Before you even look at the pieces — what is the first thing you need to fix? And after you fix it, will all the pieces still be in the right places?**

*Answer: Rotate the board 90 degrees so a light square is in the bottom-right corner ("Light on Right"). After rotating, ALL the pieces will be on wrong squares because the files and ranks have shifted — you will need to reset every piece.*

slides.title: Common Mistakes
slides.text:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Board rotated 90°** — A dark square ends up in the bottom-right corner. Fix: "Light on Right."
- ❌ **King and Queen swapped** — The most frequent error. Fix: "Queen on her own color."
- ❌ **Knights and Bishops swapped** — Knights go next to the Rooks (on b and g files), Bishops go next to the Queen and King (on c and f files).
- ❌ **Rooks not in the corners** — Rooks are always on the a-file and h-file.

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Naming all pieces at once** — This overwhelms a young child. Start with the board itself, then introduce pieces one at a time over multiple sessions if needed.
- ❌ **Correcting mistakes harshly** — Setup errors are normal. Gently guide rather than point out failures.
- ❌ **Skipping board orientation** — Many parents jump straight to pieces. Always start with "Light on Right."

- "Which corner should be light?" (Bottom-right)
- "Where does the Queen go?" (On her own color)
- "What goes in the corners?" (The Rooks)
- "How many squares are on the board?" (64)

- They place the Queen on the right square.

guide_sections.title: Definition
guide_sections.text: A chess board is a square board divided into 64 smaller squares arranged in an 8×8 grid. The squares alternate between two colors — one light, one dark. Each player sits on opposite sides of the board. The board is the playing field for every game of chess.

guide_sections.title: Parent Understands
guide_sections.text:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it. You need to know this before you can teach it.*

**The 64 Squares**
The board has exactly 64 squares: 32 light and 32 dark, arranged in an alternating checkerboard pattern. No two squares of the same color are ever next to each other (horizontally or vertically).

**Board Orientation**
This is the single most common setup mistake. The board must be placed so that **the bottom-right corner square (closest to each player's right hand) is a light-colored square**. An easy way to remember: **"Light on Right."** If the corner square on your right is dark, the board is turned the wrong way.

**Files, Ranks, and Coordinates**
- **Files** are the vertical columns running up and down the board. They are labeled **a** through **h** from left to right (from White's perspective).
- **Ranks** are the horizontal rows running side to side. They are numbered **1** through **8** from bottom to top (from White's perspective).
- Every square has a unique name made from its file letter and rank number. For example, the bottom-left corner is **a1** and the top-right corner is **h8**.

**Piece Placement**
Each side starts with 16 pieces arranged on the two ranks closest to them:
- **Rank 1 (White) / Rank 8 (Black)**: Rook, Knight, Bishop, Queen, King, Bishop, Knight, Rook.
- **Rank 2 (White) / Rank 7 (Black)**: All eight pawns.

The critical rule: **"Queen on her own color."** The White Queen goes on the light square (d1). The Black Queen goes on the dark square (d8).

guide_sections.title: How to Teach It
guide_sections.text:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — Start with the empty board (2 minutes)
Place the empty board between you and your child. Say:

> *"This is a chess board. It has 64 squares — can you see how the colors take turns? Light, dark, light, dark. Let's count one row together."*

Let them count one row (they should get 8).

### Step 2 — Teach "Light on Right" (1 minute)
Point to the bottom-right corner. Ask:

> *"What color is this corner? It should always be light. Remember: Light on Right."*

Turn the board wrong, then ask them to fix it. Repeat until they do it automatically.

### Step 3 — Introduce the corners (2 minutes)
Place one piece in each corner. Say:

> *"The Rooks — the castle towers — always go in the corners. Can you put one in each corner?"*

### Step 4 — Build from the outside in (3 minutes)
Work from corners toward center:

> *"Next to each Rook, place a Knight — the horse. Then next to each Knight, place a Bishop. Now we just have two squares left in the middle. That's where the Queen and King go."*

### Step 5 — Teach "Queen on her color" (2 minutes)
Hold up the White Queen. Point to d1:

> *"The Queen always goes on her own color. White Queen on the white square. Can you show me?"*

Do the same for the Black Queen on d8.

### Step 6 — Place the pawns (1 minute)
> *"Now fill the whole second row with pawns — the little soldiers who protect everyone."*

### Step 7 — Celebrate
> *"You just set up a chess board! Every grandmaster in the world starts their game exactly like this."*

guide_sections.title: Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint

> **🏰 The Castle Analogy**
>
> Imagine the chess board is a castle's courtyard — a big square field made of tiles. The tiles alternate between white marble and dark stone, like a grand checkerboard floor. Two armies face each other from opposite ends of the courtyard. The generals (Kings) stand in the center with their advisors (Queens), protected by towers (Rooks) in the corners, horsemen (Knights) next to the towers, and the royal guards (Bishops) beside them. In front of the whole army stands a row of brave soldiers (Pawns), ready to march forward.
>
> **Memory tricks your child will love:**
> - **"Light on Right"** — Say it every time you set up the board together.
> - **"Queen on her color"** — The White Queen likes the white tile. The Black Queen likes the dark tile.
> - **"Rooks in the corners, like castle towers"** — Rooks look like towers and they go in the corners, just like real towers on a castle wall.

guide_sections.title: Did You Know? 🎓
guide_sections.text:
The chess board we use today has been virtually unchanged for over **500 years**. The 8×8 grid was standardized in Europe during the 15th century, though chess itself is over 1,400 years old. Some early versions of the game were played on 10×10 boards! When your child sets up their board, they are continuing a tradition that stretches back centuries — longer than most countries have existed.

*Share this with your child: "Did you know this board design is over 500 years old? Even kings and queens in castles played on a board just like this one!"*

guide_sections.title: How It Works
guide_sections.text:
### Setting Up the Board — Step by Step

1. **Place the board** so that a **light square** is in the bottom-right corner ("Light on Right").
2. **Place the Rooks** in all four corners: a1, h1 (White), a8, h8 (Black).
3. **Place the Knights** next to each Rook: b1, g1 (White), b8, g8 (Black).
4. **Place the Bishops** next to each Knight: c1, f1 (White), c8, f8 (Black).
5. **Place the Queens** — "Queen on her own color": d1 (White Queen on the light square), d8 (Black Queen on the dark square).
6. **Place the Kings** on the remaining center square: e1 (White), e8 (Black).
7. **Place all Pawns** on the second rank: a2 through h2 (White), a7 through h7 (Black).

*Tip: Teach your child the order from the outside in — Rooks first (corners), then Knights, then Bishops, then Queen and King in the center.*

### Key Rules
- The board has **8 files** (columns, labeled a–h) and **8 ranks** (rows, numbered 1–8).
- **Light on Right**: The bottom-right corner must always be a light square.
- **Queen on her own color**: White Queen on a light square (d1), Black Queen on a dark square (d8).
- Both armies **mirror each other** across the board.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: A chess board is a square board divided into 64 smaller squares arranged in an 8×8 grid. The squares alternate between two colors — one light, one dark. Each player sits on opposite sides of the board. The board is the playing field for every game of chess.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.text: Every chess concept your child will ever learn happens on this board. If they cannot orient the board correctly or find specific squares, every future lesson becomes harder. Think of it this way: you would not teach someone to read without first showing them the alphabet. The chess board is the alphabet of chess. Children who are comfortable with the board learn piece movement, tactics, and strategy much faster because they are not struggling with the basics underneath.

sections.title: Parent Understands
sections.text:
*This section is for YOUR understanding. Read it, absorb it. You need to know this before you can teach it.*

**The 64 Squares**
The board has exactly 64 squares: 32 light and 32 dark, arranged in an alternating checkerboard pattern. No two squares of the same color are ever next to each other (horizontally or vertically).

**Board Orientation**
This is the single most common setup mistake. The board must be placed so that **the bottom-right corner square (closest to each player's right hand) is a light-colored square**. An easy way to remember: **"Light on Right."** If the corner square on your right is dark, the board is turned the wrong way.

**Files, Ranks, and Coordinates**
- **Files** are the vertical columns running up and down the board. They are labeled **a** through **h** from left to right (from White's perspective).
- **Ranks** are the horizontal rows running side to side. They are numbered **1** through **8** from bottom to top (from White's perspective).
- Every square has a unique name made from its file letter and rank number. For example, the bottom-left corner is **a1** and the top-right corner is **h8**.

**Piece Placement**
Each side starts with 16 pieces arranged on the two ranks closest to them:
- **Rank 1 (White) / Rank 8 (Black)**: Rook, Knight, Bishop, Queen, King, Bishop, Knight, Rook.
- **Rank 2 (White) / Rank 7 (Black)**: All eight pawns.

The critical rule: **"Queen on her own color."** The White Queen goes on the light square (d1). The Black Queen goes on the dark square (d8).

sections.title: How to Teach It
sections.text:
*Now that you understand the concept, here is exactly how to explain it to your child.*

### Step 1 — Start with the empty board (2 minutes)
Place the empty board between you and your child. Say:

> *"This is a chess board. It has 64 squares — can you see how the colors take turns? Light, dark, light, dark. Let's count one row together."*

Let them count one row (they should get 8).

### Step 2 — Teach "Light on Right" (1 minute)
Point to the bottom-right corner. Ask:

> *"What color is this corner? It should always be light. Remember: Light on Right."*

Turn the board wrong, then ask them to fix it. Repeat until they do it automatically.

### Step 3 — Introduce the corners (2 minutes)
Place one piece in each corner. Say:

> *"The Rooks — the castle towers — always go in the corners. Can you put one in each corner?"*

### Step 4 — Build from the outside in (3 minutes)
Work from corners toward center:

> *"Next to each Rook, place a Knight — the horse. Then next to each Knight, place a Bishop. Now we just have two squares left in the middle. That's where the Queen and King go."*

### Step 5 — Teach "Queen on her color" (2 minutes)
Hold up the White Queen. Point to d1:

> *"The Queen always goes on her own color. White Queen on the white square. Can you show me?"*

Do the same for the Black Queen on d8.

### Step 6 — Place the pawns (1 minute)
> *"Now fill the whole second row with pawns — the little soldiers who protect everyone."*

### Step 7 — Celebrate
> *"You just set up a chess board! Every grandmaster in the world starts their game exactly like this."*

sections.title: Teaching Story / Analogy / Memory Hint
sections.text:
> **🏰 The Castle Analogy**
>
> Imagine the chess board is a castle's courtyard — a big square field made of tiles. The tiles alternate between white marble and dark stone, like a grand checkerboard floor. Two armies face each other from opposite ends of the courtyard. The generals (Kings) stand in the center with their advisors (Queens), protected by towers (Rooks) in the corners, horsemen (Knights) next to the towers, and the royal guards (Bishops) beside them. In front of the whole army stands a row of brave soldiers (Pawns), ready to march forward.
>
> **Memory tricks your child will love:**
> - **"Light on Right"** — Say it every time you set up the board together.
> - **"Queen on her color"** — The White Queen likes the white tile. The Black Queen likes the dark tile.
> - **"Rooks in the corners, like castle towers"** — Rooks look like towers and they go in the corners, just like real towers on a castle wall.

sections.title: Did You Know? 🎓
sections.text:
The chess board we use today has been virtually unchanged for over **500 years**. The 8×8 grid was standardized in Europe during the 15th century, though chess itself is over 1,400 years old. Some early versions of the game were played on 10×10 boards! When your child sets up their board, they are continuing a tradition that stretches back centuries — longer than most countries have existed.

*Share this with your child: "Did you know this board design is over 500 years old? Even kings and queens in castles played on a board just like this one!"*

sections.title: How It Works
sections.text:
### Setting Up the Board — Step by Step

1. **Place the board** so that a **light square** is in the bottom-right corner ("Light on Right").
2. **Place the Rooks** in all four corners: a1, h1 (White), a8, h8 (Black).
3. **Place the Knights** next to each Rook: b1, g1 (White), b8, g8 (Black).
4. **Place the Bishops** next to each Knight: c1, f1 (White), c8, f8 (Black).
5. **Place the Queens** — "Queen on her own color": d1 (White Queen on the light square), d8 (Black Queen on the dark square).
6. **Place the Kings** on the remaining center square: e1 (White), e8 (Black).
7. **Place all Pawns** on the second rank: a2 through h2 (White), a7 through h7 (Black).

*Tip: Teach your child the order from the outside in — Rooks first (corners), then Knights, then Bishops, then Queen and King in the center.*

### Key Rules
- The board has **8 files** (columns, labeled a–h) and **8 ranks** (rows, numbered 1–8).
- **Light on Right**: The bottom-right corner must always be a light square.
- **Queen on her own color**: White Queen on a light square (d1), Black Queen on a dark square (d8).
- Both armies **mirror each other** across the board.

sections.title: Real Game Example
sections.text:
**Every chess game ever played in history started from this exact position.**

In the 2013 World Chess Championship between Magnus Carlsen and Viswanathan Anand, the board was set up exactly as shown in Diagram 1 — with "Light on Right" and "Queen on her own color." Whether it is a game between two world champions or your child's first game at the kitchen table, the starting position is always the same.

This is one of the beautiful things about chess: the rules have been the same for hundreds of years. When your child sets up the board correctly, they are doing the exact same thing that every grandmaster has done.

*Tell your child: "You just set up the board the same way Magnus Carlsen does. That's pretty cool."*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.text:
### Chess Mistakes
- ❌ **Board rotated 90°** — A dark square ends up in the bottom-right corner. Fix: "Light on Right."
- ❌ **King and Queen swapped** — The most frequent error. Fix: "Queen on her own color."
- ❌ **Knights and Bishops swapped** — Knights go next to the Rooks (on b and g files), Bishops go next to the Queen and King (on c and f files).
- ❌ **Rooks not in the corners** — Rooks are always on the a-file and h-file.

### Teaching Mistakes
- ❌ **Naming all pieces at once** — This overwhelms a young child. Start with the board itself, then introduce pieces one at a time over multiple sessions if needed.
- ❌ **Correcting mistakes harshly** — Setup errors are normal. Gently guide rather than point out failures.
- ❌ **Skipping board orientation** — Many parents jump straight to pieces. Always start with "Light on Right."

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> If your child keeps swapping the King and Queen, try this: let them place only the Queen first, every time, before any other piece. Once the Queen is on her color, the King automatically gets the only square left. This builds the habit faster than correcting the mistake.

sections.title: Teaching Notes
sections.text:
**For the parent / coach:**

- **Teach this before** introducing any piece movement. The board must feel familiar first.
- **Use a physical board first.** Screen-based boards are fine later, but the tactile experience of picking up pieces and placing them helps young children remember.
- **Let your child touch and explore.** Let them pick up pieces, feel them, and ask questions before you start the "lesson."
- **Break it into sessions if needed.** Session 1: Board orientation and squares. Session 2: Piece placement. There is no rush.

**Questions to ask your child:**
- "Which corner should be light?" (Bottom-right)
- "Where does the Queen go?" (On her own color)
- "What goes in the corners?" (The Rooks)
- "How many squares are on the board?" (64)

**Signs your child understands:**
- They orient the board correctly without help.
- They place the Queen on the right square.
- They say "Light on Right" unprompted.

**Signs they need more practice:**
- They consistently place the Queen on the wrong square.
- They rotate the board incorrectly.
- They confuse Knights and Bishops.

> **🧑‍🏫 Coach Tip:**
> The single best drill for this topic is the "blind setup" — cover the board with a cloth, ask your child to set up one side from memory, then reveal and check together. This moves knowledge from recognition to recall.

sections.title: Parent FAQ
sections.text:
**Q: My child keeps placing the board wrong. Should I keep correcting them?**
A: Yes, gently. Say "Let's check — Light on Right!" and let them fix it themselves. Avoid saying "That's wrong." Instead, make it a quick game: "Quick quiz — is this corner light?" Within a few sessions, they will self-correct automatically.

**Q: Do I need to teach coordinates (a1, b2, etc.) right away?**
A: Not immediately. Your child should first be comfortable with the board itself — its colors, its orientation, and where the pieces go. Coordinates are a separate topic (TOP-006) that builds on this one. Introduce them naturally over time ("Can you put the Rook on a1?") rather than as a formal lesson.

**Q: Is it okay to start with fewer pieces?**
A: Absolutely. Many coaches start by placing only pawns, or only Rooks and Kings. This reduces overwhelm and lets the child focus on fewer things at once. The full 32-piece setup is the goal, not the starting point.

sections.title: Practice Together
sections.text:
*These activities are designed for parent and child to do together. No scores. No pressure. Just learning.*

### 🏁 Speed Setup Race
Both parent and child each get a set of pieces. Race to set up the board correctly. The goal is not to win — it is to practice together. Cheer each other on.

### 🔍 Find the Square
Point to any square and ask your child to name it (or vice versa). Start with corners (a1, h1, a8, h8), then try center squares (d4, e5). Use the coordinates diagram below for reference.

### 🎨 Color Check
Remove all pieces. Point to random squares and ask: "Is this square light or dark?" Then try: "Can you find d4? What color is it?"

### 🪞 Mirror Game
Set up only White's pieces. Ask your child to "mirror" them on Black's side. This reinforces that both sides are identical reflections of each other.

### 👑 Queen Challenge
Remove just the Queens and Kings. Ask your child to place them correctly. If they say "Queen on her own color" before you do — they have mastered the most important setup rule.

sections.title: Coach Challenge ⭐
sections.text:
### 🏆 The 60-Second Setup Challenge

**Challenge your child:**

> "Can you set up the entire board correctly in under 60 seconds?"

**Rules:**
1. Start with an empty board and all 32 pieces in a pile.
2. The parent times with a phone or watch.
3. The child sets up the board.
4. When done, the parent checks: "Light on Right? Queen on her own color? Rooks in the corners?"
5. If everything is correct, record their time.

**Make it fun:**
- First attempt: just get it right, no time pressure.
- Second attempt: try to beat your first time.
- Track improvement over days — children love seeing their time drop.

*This is PCA original content. This challenge builds muscle memory for board setup while making it a game rather than a chore.*

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.text:
### 🟢 Recognition (Easy)
**Look at the diagram below. Something is wrong with White's setup. Can you spot the mistake?**

*Answer: The White King and Queen are swapped. The Queen should be on d1 (light square) and the King should be on e1 (dark square). Remember: "Queen on her own color."*

### 🟡 Application (Medium)
**Without looking at any diagram, answer these three questions:**
1. What are the four corner squares of the board?
2. What color is the square h1?
3. Which piece goes on a1?

*Answers: (1) a1, h1, a8, h8. (2) Light. (3) The Rook.*

### 🔴 Challenge (Hard)
**Your board has a dark square in the bottom-right corner. You have placed all 32 pieces perfectly on the board. Before you even look at the pieces — what is the first thing you need to fix? And after you fix it, will all the pieces still be in the right places?**

*Answer: Rotate the board 90 degrees so a light square is in the bottom-right corner ("Light on Right"). After rotating, ALL the pieces will be on wrong squares because the files and ranks have shifted — you will need to reset every piece.*
